sections.title: Overview
blocks: A **hypertrophic scar** is a raised scar that stays **within** the original wound and often improves over 1–2 years. A **keloid** is firm scar tissue that grows **beyond** the original wound border, persists and often recurs after excision.

sub: Keloids peak at 10–30 years; up to 15–20× more common in people of African descent.

ul: Excess collagen production with reduced breakdown during wound healing.
Triggers: acne, piercing, surgery (especially under tension), burns, vaccination, minor trauma.
**Keloids** are much more common in **skin of colour** and run in families.
**"Cut it out and it's gone"**: keloids recur in most cases after simple excision.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Raised scars come from **too much collagen** and not enough breakdown.

mech.t: Injury starts normal healing: inflammation, proliferation, remodelling.
TGF-β signalling keeps fibroblasts producing collagen.
Hypertrophic scars stay in the wound; keloids invade surrounding skin with thick, glassy collagen.

mech.t: Wounds under tension (chest, shoulders) are most prone.

histo: Keloid: thick hyalinised (glassy) collagen bundles; hypertrophic scar: nodules of collagen parallel to the surface.

sections.title: Management

ul: Prevention: avoid elective procedures (piercing, cosmetic surgery) on keloid-prone sites in people with a keloid history.
**Silicone gel or sheet** (OTC) for months, not weeks; pressure (earlobe pressure clips).
Potent topical steroid under occlusion for early raised scars.
Specialist: **intralesional steroid**, cryotherapy, pulsed dye laser, careful excision with adjuvant therapy (**high recurrence** after excision alone).

blocks: Explain that the aim is **improvement, not removal**.
